name: Horizon Europe
evidence_rating: moderate: strong causal evidence that predecessor (Horizon 2020) grants help firms; Horizon Europe's own GDP and jobs effects only model-based so far
summary: Horizon Europe, the EU's EUR 93.5 billion research programme, was forecast to return up to EUR 11 in GDP for every euro spent over 25 years and create up to 100,000 research jobs. Its 2025 interim evaluation says it is on track, but those figures come from re-running economic models; measured results so far are about 40,000 jobs reported by a fifth of projects and EUR 10 billion of co-investment. Rigorous studies of its predecessor find that grants helped small firms invest, patent and grow, while European Research Council grants made little difference to researchers just above the funding line.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement has no LFS indicators (1.4.2-1.4.4 empty in extraction); monitoring is through 'key impact pathway' indicators (Annex V of the Regulation), annual monitoring and interim/ex-post evaluations

indicators.indicator: Average GDP gain of 0.08-0.19% over 25 years; each euro invested returns up to EUR 11 of GDP
indicators.target_or_baseline: +0.08-0.19% GDP; up to EUR 11 per EUR 1
indicators.evidence: Model-based only: interim evaluation's NEMESIS, RHOMOLO and FIDELIO runs give GDP multipliers of 4-11 by 2045 and say results are on track (RHOMOLO peak +0.10% of GDP in 2024). These re-run the same type of models used ex ante; no observed macro effect.

indicators.indicator: Up to 100,000 direct R&I jobs in 2021-2027 and up to 200,000 indirect jobs in 2027-2036
indicators.evidence: Reported: 39,543 FTE jobs created or maintained by participants (data from only 21% of projects, Jan 2025); NEMESIS estimates up to 60,000 research jobs by 2023-24; RHOMOLO about 128,000 persons (+0.06%) at 2023 peak.
Measured: EUR 10.2bn co-investment by participants by the interim evaluation, against just over EUR 5bn at the same stage of Horizon 2020.

indicators.indicator: Success rates and funding of high-quality proposals
indicators.evidence: Measured: average success rate rose from 12% (Horizon 2020) to 16.4%; only 30.1% of high-quality proposals funded (25% in Horizon 2020) - funding all would have required an extra EUR 81.8bn. 15,148 grants worth EUR 43.2bn signed 2021-2024; budget cut from EUR 95.5bn to 93.5bn in 2024.

indicators.indicator: Higher growth of SMEs, more scale-ups and breakthrough innovation
indicators.evidence: No causal estimate yet for Horizon Europe. For its predecessor (Horizon 2020) quasi-experimental studies find positive effects: SME Instrument grants raised investment, patents and survival (regression discontinuity); Horizon 2020 grantees grew employment ~20% and assets/revenue ~30% vs high-quality rejected applicants (difference-in-differences).
indicators.sources: Santoleri et al. 2024; Mitra & Niakaros 2023; SWD(2024) 29

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for Horizon Europe (executive summary SWD(2018) 308), SWD(2018) 307
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for Horizon Europe (executive summary SWD(2018) 308)
literature.method: ex-ante (QUEST, RHOMOLO and NEMESIS macro models)
literature.headline: Continuation scenario: average GDP increase of 0.08-0.19% over 25 years, up to EUR 11 of GDP per euro invested; up to 100,000 direct R&I jobs in 2021-2027 and up to 200,000 indirect jobs in 2027-2036; Horizon Europe changes add +0.04% to +0.1% of GDP (EUR 800-975bn over 25 years)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission forecast that Horizon Europe would add up to EUR 11 to EU output for every euro spent over 25 years and create up to 100,000 research jobs during the programme.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Ex-post evaluation of Horizon 2020, the EU Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (Staff Working Document), SWD(2024) 29
literature.title: Ex-post evaluation of Horizon 2020, the EU Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (Staff Working Document)
literature.method: ex-post evaluation; synthesis incl. counterfactual studies and macro models
literature.headline: Counterfactual studies show positive causal effects on beneficiary firms (employment +20%, assets and revenues ~+30%; SME Instrument beneficiaries attracted 46-97% more follow-on investment); macro models put peak GDP gain at +0.18-0.25% and total gains to 2040 at EUR 429bn (RHOMOLO), below the interim evaluation's expectations except in NEMESIS
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's final evaluation of Horizon 2020 found funded firms grew faster than similar rejected applicants, while model-based GDP gains came in lower than previously expected in two of three models.
literature.quality: mixed: some causal firm-level studies plus models

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Interim Evaluation of the Horizon Europe Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (2021-2024), SWD(2025) 110
literature.title: Interim Evaluation of the Horizon Europe Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (2021-2024)
literature.method: interim evaluation; monitoring data and macro-model simulations (NEMESIS, RHOMOLO, FIDELIO)
literature.headline: 39,543 FTE jobs created or maintained (21% of projects reporting); EUR 10.2bn co-investment; GDP multiplier of 4-11 by 2045 and 'on track' vs the IA; success rate 16.4% but 7 in 10 high-quality proposals unfunded
literature.summary_plain: The interim evaluation says Horizon Europe is on track, but its growth estimates are model re-runs and 7 in 10 high-quality proposals go unfunded.
literature.quality: monitoring and models; no counterfactual on Horizon Europe yet
literature.verified: full text read (impact and efficiency sections)

literature.citation: Santoleri, P., Mina, A., Di Minin, A. & Martelli, I. (2024), The Causal Effects of R&D Grants: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity, Review of Economics and Statistics 106(6): 1495-1510
literature.authors: Santoleri, P., Mina, A., Di Minin, A. & Martelli, I.
literature.title: The Causal Effects of R&D Grants: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity
literature.method: regression discontinuity (Horizon 2020 SME Instrument evaluation scores)
literature.headline: Grants trigger sizable impacts on firm outcomes, consistent with reduced financial frictions; effect due to funding, not certification ('Seal of Excellence' quality stamps alone do not improve performance); private returns comparable to US SBIR; spillovers via higher entrepreneurial entry. Commission evaluation cites 15-31% more citation-weighted patents
literature.summary_plain: A rigorous study of the EU's SME Instrument found that winning a grant (rather than just a quality label) made small firms invest, patent and grow more and made them less likely to fail.

literature.citation: Mitra, A. & Niakaros, K. (European Commission, DG RTD) (2023), The Horizon effect: A counterfactual analysis of EU research & innovation grants, Publications Office of the EU (R&I Paper Series)
literature.authors: Mitra, A. & Niakaros, K. (European Commission, DG RTD)
literature.title: The Horizon effect: A counterfactual analysis of EU research & innovation grants
literature.venue: Publications Office of the EU (R&I Paper Series)
literature.headline: Firms receiving a first Horizon 2020 grant increased employment by about 20% and total assets and revenues by about 30% relative to comparable non-funded applicants with high-quality proposals; effects concentrated in ICT and professional/scientific services, insignificant elsewhere
literature.summary_plain: Commission economists found companies that won Horizon 2020 grants grew jobs by about a fifth and revenue by about 30% compared with similar firms that narrowly missed out, mostly in tech and professional services.
literature.interested_party: Authors are European Commission (DG Research and Innovation) staff evaluating their own programme

literature.citation: Ghirelli, C., Havari, E., Meroni, E. & Verzillo, S. (2023), The Long-Term Causal Effects of Winning an ERC Grant, IZA Discussion Paper 16108 / Banco de España Working Paper 2313
literature.authors: Ghirelli, C., Havari, E., Meroni, E. & Verzillo, S.
literature.title: The Long-Term Causal Effects of Winning an ERC Grant
literature.venue: IZA Discussion Paper 16108 / Banco de España Working Paper 2313
literature.method: regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences (all ERC applicants 2007-2013, Scopus records)
literature.outcomes: scientific productivity; citation impact; further EU funding
literature.headline: Near the funding cut-off (RD) no significant effect on productivity or quality; DiD on broader population finds positive long-term effects in some fields (Chemistry, Universe and Earth Sciences, Medicine, etc.), driven by top-ranked applicants
literature.summary_plain: A study of European Research Council grants found winning made no measurable difference to the output of researchers just above the funding line, though top-ranked winners in some fields did gain.
